subject: typescript
title: Types
description: Annotations, inference, literal and union types, and why any defeats the point.

content.title: Definition
content.body: A type describes the set of values an expression may hold. TypeScript checks those descriptions at compile time and then erases them — nothing about types survives into the emitted JavaScript.

content.title: Inference beats annotation
content.body: Annotate function parameters and public boundaries; let TypeScript infer the rest. Redundant annotations go stale.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: any switches checking off for everything it touches. unknown is the safe counterpart: you must narrow it before use.

exercises.question: What type does TypeScript infer for name?
exercises.explanation: A const binding cannot be reassigned, so the narrowest useful type is the literal. let name = "Anna" would widen to string.

exercises.question: What is the practical difference between any and unknown?

answers.text: They are aliases for the same type
unknown must be narrowed before you can use it; any allows any operation unchecked
any is a runtime check, unknown is compile time

exercises.explanation: Both accept any value on the way in. Only unknown forces you to prove what it is before reading from it, which is why it belongs on API boundaries.

exercises.question: Complete the annotation so the parameter accepts both a string and a number.
exercises.explanation: | forms a union (either type). & forms an intersection, which would require a value that is both at once.

exercises.question: Which line does the compiler reject?

answers.text: Line 3 — a string is not assignable to number
Line 2 — push is not allowed on a typed array
Line 4 — length needs a type assertion
Line 1 — an array annotation must use Array<number>

exercises.explanation: number[] constrains every element, and push is typed accordingly. Note that const only freezes the binding, not the contents.

exercises.question: TypeScript types are available at runtime and can be inspected with typeof.
exercises.explanation: Types are erased during compilation. typeof is JavaScript's runtime operator and knows nothing about your interfaces or unions.

exercises.question: Which annotation restricts a value to exactly three named states?
exercises.explanation: A union of string literals is the idiomatic way to model a closed set of states, and it narrows cleanly in a switch.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Without an annotation, const ids = [] is inferred as ___[].
exercises.explanation: An empty array literal starts as any[] and TypeScript widens it from later pushes — under noImplicitAny in a non-evolving position it is an error instead.

exercises.question: Syntax
exercises.back: Tells the compiler to trust you — no runtime check happens
exercises.explanation: An assertion silences the checker without validating anything. If you are wrong, the failure surfaces later and further away.

exercises.question: Why does the compiler reject line 2?

answers.text: toUpperCase does not exist on number, so it is unavailable until x is narrowed
A union type cannot be a parameter

exercises.explanation: On a union you may only use members shared by every constituent. A typeof guard makes the string branch safe.

exercises.question: What are the inferred types of a and b?
exercises.explanation: A let binding can be reassigned, so TypeScript widens the literal to its base type. const cannot, so the literal survives — which is what makes const the better default for union discriminants.

exercises.question: What changes when strictNullChecks is turned on?

answers.text: null and undefined stop being assignable to every type and must be in the union explicitly
Every variable must be initialised at declaration
Optional properties are no longer allowed
null checks are inserted at runtime

exercises.explanation: Without it, string silently includes null. With it, string | null is a different type, and the compiler forces the check before you dereference.

exercises.question: Complete the assertion so LEVELS becomes a readonly tuple of literals rather than string[].
exercises.explanation: as const freezes the literals, which is how you derive a union from an array: type Level = (typeof LEVELS)[number].

exercises.question: The satisfies operator checks a value against a type without widening the value's own inferred type.
exercises.explanation: That is the whole point: a config object can be validated against Record<string, string> while keeping its exact keys for autocomplete.

exercises.question: This compiles and crashes at runtime. Which line is responsible?

answers.text: Line 3 — toUpperCase does not exist on string
Line 2 — the assertion tells the compiler to trust unvalidated data

exercises.explanation: json() returns any (or unknown). An assertion is a promise you make to the compiler; validating the payload is the only thing that makes it true.

exercises.question: What does `A & B` describe for two object types?

answers.text: A value that has the members of both
A value that is either A or B
Only the members A and B have in common
An error, since objects cannot be intersected

exercises.explanation: Unions restrict what you may read; intersections combine what is present. Intersecting conflicting primitive members produces never.
